title: How the Hoover Dam Works, Part II
summary: Part two of the Hoover Dam story. The hosts cover the Hoover Dam Bypass bridge and its pedestrian walkway, Lake Mead's size and recreation, the dam's stats and power output, the four diversion tunnels repurposed as penstocks for hydroelectric generation and as spillways, the 1941 spillway test and 1983 flood use, cavitation damage and aeration fixes, seepage and the grout curtain, the dam's impact on regional agriculture, wartime security including the 1939 reported German bombing plot and closure after Pearl Harbor, post-9/11 security and escorted crossings, the ongoing drought and falling Lake Mead levels with the new low-level pumping system, a proposed LADWP solar pump-back loop, and the Dam's dedication star map. The episode closes with listener mail about a tuba-flatulence anecdote involving Oliver! and the song "Food, Glorious Food."
topics: drought and Lake Mead water levels

entities.name: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power

segments.title: Cold open and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck promotes a New York live performance with Beth Newell and Pete McNerney, then Josh introduces the episode as part two of Hoover Dam.

segments.title: Old highway and the Hoover Dam bypass bridge
segments.summary: The hosts describe the finished dam roadway, the old two-lane road over the dam, and the bypass bridge that spans the Black Canyon, including its low railing and pedestrian walkway and views of rainbows from the spray.

segments.title: Construction finish and Lake Mead
segments.summary: The dam was finished under budget and two years early, with project manager Frank Crowe credited with saving eight million dollars. Lake Mead formed behind the dam, and the hosts discuss its size, visitors, and acre-foot measurement.

segments.title: Dam statistics and power output
segments.summary: The hosts compare Hoover Dam's height with the Oroville/Oroville-like Aurora dam ranking, note its rank as second in the US and eleventh in the world for power production, and discuss how much of Los Angeles County's and the region's power it supplies and how it is distributed.

segments.title: Diversion tunnels as penstocks and power generation
segments.summary: The four diversion tunnels used to divert the river were kept; two were encased in steel and reduced in diameter to serve as penstocks feeding turbines in the power stations on the Nevada and Arizona sides. Water flows by gravity from Lake Mead through intake towers, and the hosts discuss flow rates and horsepower.

segments.title: Spillways and the 1941 and 1983 tests
segments.summary: The two remaining diversion tunnels were converted into spillways to route floodwater past the power stations if water rose within 27 feet of the crest. The spillways were tested in 1941 and used during a 1983 flood, and they suffered damage each time.

segments.title: Cavitation damage and aeration fix
segments.summary: High-velocity water in the spillways created cavitation bubbles whose collapse sheared away chunks of concrete. Air ducts for aeration were installed afterward to cushion the impact; the government had initially denied funds for them in 1941.

segments.title: Seepage, uplift, and the grout curtain
segments.summary: Seepage under the dam base created uplift pressure, which the hosts attribute to poor geological exploration before construction. Engineers pressure-injected grout into bedrock fissures and drilled further to build a grout curtain beneath the dam.

segments.title: Regional impact: agriculture, Las Vegas, and Tucson
segments.summary: Flood control and reliable irrigation let the region's agriculture grow, making it a major source of US crops and livestock and leading to the nickname America's salad bowl. The hosts also name Boulder City, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, and Tucson as beneficiaries.

segments.title: Wartime security and the 1939 bombing plot
segments.summary: In 1939 the Mexican government reportedly warned that Germans planned to bomb the dam, prompting new safeguards such as military police, floodlights, and a steel net on Lake Mead. The dam was closed to the public after Pearl Harbor until the mid-1990s. Post-9/11 vehicles were escorted across the old road until the bypass opened.

segments.title: Drought, low Lake Mead, and water supply
segments.summary: Roughly sixteen years of drought have lowered Lake Mead by about 150 feet, cutting off hydro intakes and water intakes. A new low-level pumping station under the lake now draws water. Climate change and evaporation are cited as ongoing concerns.

segments.title: Proposed solar pump-back loop
segments.summary: The LA Department of Water and Power has proposed a solar-powered pump station downstream to send water back up to Lake Mead, which could boost generation and store electricity. Downstream water users object because they depend on the water.

segments.title: Dedication and star map
segments.summary: Franklin Roosevelt dedicated the dam, and Herbert Hoover was not invited. The sculptor Oscar J. W. Hansen's Art Deco statues stand on site, and the terrazzo floor features a star map of the sky on the dedication date.

segments.title: Listener mail: Oliver! and tuba flatulence
segments.summary: A listener from Denver recalls playing the flatulent orphan in a childhood production of Oliver! during Food Glorious Food, correcting the hosts' attribution of that song after a Desert Survival episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite contact via the website or email, and close with the show credits.
